"
Northern Territory police failed to act on a string of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles before the death of a vulnerable 23-year-old man last year, a coroner has found. NT coroner Greg Cavanagh has criticised police for failing to act on an internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged vehicles in 2013, following an earlier death in custody. In the three years between the two deaths, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in caged vehicles. “In six cases the persons were not detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious,” Cavanagh found. “It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.”

On 16 September last year, two officers were making their way through Darwin, on their way to investigate a noise complaint, when they came across the scene of a serious crash. A Toyota Hilux had smashed into a palm tree on the corner of the Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, not far from Darwin airport. Hiding behind some vegetation was Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23. Walkinshaw was unharmed but held his passenger in his arms. The young woman, whom he had met earlier at a bar, was in and out of consciousness, having suffered an injury to her back. Walkinshaw was well over the limit, returning a reading of 0.149.

The world for Dale had shrunk to the space between his arms, the scent of hibiscus from the crushed bushes, and the shallow, ragged breaths of the woman he was holding. He didn't register the police cruiser pulling up, not until the beams of their torches cut through the gloom and found him.

“Stay where you are!” one of the officers commanded.

Dale looked up, his face a mask of panic and booze-fueled confusion. He was just a kid, really, his broad shoulders trembling. He tried to explain—the night out, the new friend, the swerve to avoid something on the road, the sickening thud. But the words came out in a slurred jumble as paramedics gently took the woman from his arms and strapped her to a backboard. He watched her go, a stranger he’d tried to protect after he’d put her in peril, her face pale under the flashing red and blue lights.

Then the focus was entirely on him. The breathalyzer, the click of the handcuffs, the stern, procedural questions. The reading of 0.149 sealed his fate. He was clumsy and compliant, shame radiating off him in waves. They guided him to the back of the police van, a metal box on wheels.

The heavy door slammed shut, the sound echoing with a finality that shook him. He was in the cage. It was pitch black, hot, and smelled of stale sweat and disinfectant. He rattled the mesh, but there was no give. Through the small grille, he could barely make out the silhouettes of the two officers in the front, their voices a low, indifferent murmur. They were talking about the original noise complaint, their shift, anything but the man in the back.

For Dale, the darkness wasn't empty. It was filled with screeching tires, a woman’s pained moan, and the future he had just obliterated. He saw the courtroom, the prison cell, the disappointment on his family's faces. He was 23 years old, and his life was over. The cage surrounding him felt like a coffin, and the slow, rumbling journey through Darwin felt like his funeral procession.

He thought of the 2013 report he’d never read, of the sixteen silent screams in similar cages that no one had heard. He didn't know he was a statistic in the making, the inevitable answer to a question no one in power had bothered to ask urgently enough. He only knew the suffocating despair. The van was a void, and he felt a desperate, overwhelming need to disappear with it. In the suffocating, unobserved darkness, he began to work at the fabric of his shirt.

Up front, the officers took a call, their attention diverted. They drove on, unaware of the silent, desperate struggle unfolding just feet behind them.

When they arrived at the station and finally swung open the heavy rear door, the hot night air rushed into the stale compartment. Dale was slumped in the corner, motionless. They hadn't seen a thing. They hadn’t heard a thing. They were too late. As one officer frantically called for medical assistance, the other could only stare into the empty, darkened cage, a space built without eyes, a space that had just swallowed another life.

Months later, Coroner Greg Cavanagh would look over the details of the case, his face grim. He would see not just Dale Scott Walkinshaw, but the ghosts of sixteen others who had come before him, the ignored warnings, the filed-away reports. It wasn't a matter of if. For Dale, a vulnerable 23-year-old on the worst night of his life, it had simply been a matter of when.
